topic.original: "The United States Congress should establish a National AI Injury Compensation Program (NAIICP), modeled on the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP), to grant limited liability immunity to AI developers in exchange for a mandatory excise tax and adherence to tiered federal safety standards." The Logical Framework: The Noise Thesis: Ground the affirmative case for maximizing the rate of AI development and adoption in the work of Kahneman, Sibony, and Sunstein. Professional human judgment is inherently "noisy" (unwanted variability); auditable AI reduces this noise and improves accuracy to decrease harm. The Liability Chill: Current unlimited liability and the power disparity between tech giants and individuals throttle the deployment of beneficial AI. The Mechanism: An excise tax on AI services, tiered by risk (e.g., healthcare vs. social media) and safety compliance levels (basic safety vs state of the art safety practices), funds AI safety research, auditing, and a no-fault administrative compensation board. Companies that do not adhere to safety standards are not covered and are not protected from unlimited liability. Compliance must be verified by hardware-level telemetry and cryptographically verifiable audit trails, overseen by an independent, multi-disciplinary administrative board armed with federal subpoena power.

scope.core_proposition: Whether the United States Congress should establish a VICP-modeled, no-fault National AI Injury Compensation Program that grants AI developers limited liability immunity in exchange for a mandatory risk-tiered excise tax and verified adherence to tiered federal safety standards
relevant_disciplines: vaccine injury compensation policy (VICP and the 1986 National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act)
law and economics (deterrence, moral hazard, risk allocation)
public finance and excise tax design
insurance economics and actuarial risk pooling (compensation fund solvency)
behavioral decision science — noise and judgment variability (Kahneman, Sibony, Sunstein)
AI safety assurance, auditing, and compliance standards engineering
applied cryptography and hardware telemetry for verification systems
health economics and medical AI evaluation (diagnostic accuracy and variability)
US legislative process and statutory design
on_scope_evidence: VICP operational data: petition volumes, adjudication timelines, payout totals, administrative costs, and its per-dose vaccine excise tax financing model
NCVIA (1986) legislative history and the design dynamics of the vaccine injury table
comparator no-fault regimes: Price-Anderson Act nuclear liability, 9/11 Victim Compensation Fund, workers' compensation systems
empirical noise studies: inter-judge variability in medicine, sentencing, underwriting, and hiring, and measured effects of algorithmic decision support on consistency and accuracy
medical error and diagnostic variability statistics quantifying harm from human judgment noise
documented AI injury incidents: medical AI misdiagnosis cases, algorithmic denial of benefits or care, autonomous system accidents (e.g., AI Incident Database entries)
AI liability insurance market data: premiums, coverage exclusions, insurer withdrawal from AI risk classes
litigation cost asymmetry and chilling-effect evidence: AI tort defense costs versus individual plaintiff resources; documented decisions not to deploy beneficial AI due to liability exposure
excise tax incidence analysis and revenue projections for a tax on AI services
safety standard tiering precedents: FDA device classification, NIST AI RMF maturity tiers, EU AI Act risk categories
feasibility, cost, and attack-surface data for hardware-level telemetry and cryptographically verifiable audit trails
regulatory capture literature and performance records of independent oversight boards with subpoena power
key_tensions: Liability chill vs. moral hazard: accelerationists argue unlimited liability blocks deployment of noise-reducing AI that would prevent human-judgment harm; skeptics argue immunity erodes deterrence, socializes AI risk, and privatizes AI profit

Administrability of the VICP analogy: vaccines present a narrow, well-characterized injury set with known causal pathways, while AI harms are heterogeneous, diffuse, and contested — can risk tiers and a no-fault board actually adjudicate them?

The noise thesis as acceleration warrant: whether evidence that auditable AI reduces judgment variability justifies maximizing adoption rates, or whether such evidence fails to generalize to high-stakes, open-ended domains

Verification and capture: whether hardware telemetry plus cryptographic audit trails can deliver trustworthy compliance, or whether the federally funded board is captured or outmaneuvered by incumbents while tiered compliance costs entrench tech giants over smaller developers
off_scope_topics: vaccine safety and efficacy controversies (anti-vax arguments) beyond the VICP's structural design
Section 230 and platform content moderation immunity
existential risk or AGI takeover scenarios not reducible to discrete compensable injuries
international AI treaties and non-US regimes (e.g., the merits of the EU AI Act on their own)
antitrust and Big Tech market power remedies unconnected to the liability-for-tax-and-standards exchange
labor displacement and automation economics absent an injury or liability link
general tort reform debates (medical malpractice caps, asbestos trusts) without the AI or VICP-analogy connection
drift_signatures: arguing vaccine safety or vaccine-injury causation disputes rather than the VICP's compensation architecture
pivoting to Section 230 or content moderation litigation instead of product-injury liability
invoking existential or AGI-scale harms that a no-fault injury board could not adjudicate or compensate
litigating the methodology of Kahneman/Sibony/Sunstein noise research without linking it to AI-versus-human judgment tradeoffs in deployment decisions
generic Big Tech criticism (market share, data privacy, election effects) with no tie to the immunity-for-tax-and-standards mechanism
evaluating the EU AI Act or international coordination as if the actor were not specifically the United States Congress
debating medical malpractice caps or generic tort reform without connecting to AI liability or the VICP analogy
scope.example_ceiling: Severe but discrete, documentable injuries — medical AI misdiagnosis harming a patient, algorithmic denial of benefits or care, autonomous-system accidents causing individual injury or death — plus bounded systemic effects such as insurer withdrawal from AI liability markets or sector-wide deployment freezes; speculative mass-casualty or civilizational-scale AI scenarios without identifiable injured claimants exceed scope because the mechanism compensates discrete injuries
scope.domain: US federal AI liability and administrative compensation policy
scope.product_type: AI services across risk-tiered sectors (e.g., healthcare AI, social media AI)
scope.time_horizon: near-term — present-day US legislative action affecting current-generation AI deployment (inferred; no capability timeline stated)
excluded_scenarios: non-compliant AI developers — verbatim exclusion: 'Companies that do not adhere to safety standards are not covered and are not protected from unlimited liability'
immunity for non-developer actors (deployers, integrators, end users) — the topic grants immunity only to AI developers
non-US jurisdictions or international bodies — the sole specified actor is the United States Congress
harms not reducible to discrete compensable injuries (diffuse societal effects, existential-scale risk) — implied by the no-fault injury board design
explicit_qualifiers: modeled on the National Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP)
maximizing the rate of AI development and adoption
tiered by risk (e.g., healthcare vs. social media)
safety compliance levels (basic safety vs state of the art safety practices)
independent, multi-disciplinary administrative board armed with federal subpoena power
Companies that do not adhere to safety standards are not covered and are not protected from unlimited liability
